title: Unit 2: Period 2: 1607–1754

topics.name: European colonization and the regions of British America

guide.title: Period 2 (1607–1754): review guide
guide.intro: In Period 2, Spain, France, the Netherlands, and Britain built colonies with very different goals, economies, and relationships with American Indians. British colonies grew into distinct regions tied to an Atlantic economy that depended increasingly on enslaved labor.

sections.title: European colonization and British regions
body: Spain sought wealth and Catholic converts and relied on forced Native labor; the Pueblo Revolt (1680) drove the Spanish from New Mexico for over a decade. France and the Netherlands built trading colonies with relatively few settlers, forming alliances and intermarrying with American Indians. Britain sent many more settlers, including whole families.

British colonies formed distinct regions: New England's family farms, towns, and Puritan churches; the Middle Colonies' diverse population and grain exports; the Chesapeake's tobacco plantations, first worked by indentured servants and later by enslaved Africans; and the Southern colonies and West Indies, where large plantations depended on enslaved labor. Colonists developed self-government, from the Mayflower Compact (1620) to elected assemblies. Comparing these regions and empires is a key skill.
points: Compare: Spanish (conversion, labor) vs. French/Dutch (trade, alliance) vs. British (settlement, land).
Bacon's Rebellion (1676) helped push Chesapeake planters toward enslaved labor.

sections.title: Atlantic trade, slavery, and American Indians
body: An Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas. Britain's mercantilist Navigation Acts tried to keep colonial trade within the empire. Enslaved Africans were forced across the Atlantic to work on plantations; colonial laws made slavery a lifelong, inherited status passed through the mother, and enslaved people resisted through work slowdowns, escape, and revolts such as the Stono Rebellion (1739).

Relations with American Indians combined trade, alliance, conflict, and displacement. As British settlers expanded, conflicts such as Metacom's War (King Philip's War, 1675–1676) devastated both sides.
points: Slavery became racialized and hereditary through colonial laws.
Mercantilism: colonies exist to enrich the home country.

sections.title: Colonial society and culture
body: The Enlightenment spread ideas about reason and natural rights, while the Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) brought emotional revivals that challenged established churches. Both encouraged colonists to question authority.
Under salutary neglect, Britain loosely enforced trade laws, and colonial assemblies grew used to governing themselves, which would matter greatly after 1754.
points: The Great Awakening crossed colonial lines and weakened church hierarchies.
Self-government grew from long practice, not just from ideas.

example.prompt: Compare the labor systems of the Chesapeake and New England in the 1600s.
example.solution: The Chesapeake's tobacco economy relied first on indentured servants and increasingly on enslaved Africans; New England's economy of family farms, fishing, and trade relied mainly on family labor, though slavery existed there too.

misconceptions: “Slavery was the same everywhere from the start.”
It developed over time, becoming hereditary and racialized through colonial laws.
“All European colonizers treated American Indians the same way.”
The French and Dutch relied more on trade and alliance; the British sought land.
They developed elected assemblies, but voting was limited to some property-owning men.
“The Great Awakening was only about religion.”
It also encouraged challenges to established authority.

passages.title: Source A: The Mayflower Compact, 1620
text: “We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James . . . Having undertaken, for the Glory of God, and advancements of the Christian faith and honor of our King and Country, a voyage to plant the first colony in the Northern parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God, and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic; for our better ordering, and preservation and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof to enact, constitute, and frame, such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and offices, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the colony; unto which we promise all due submission and obedience.”
passages.attribution: The Mayflower Compact, signed by male passengers of the Mayflower before landing at Plymouth, 1620. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 3.3.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/3-3-english-settlements-in-america); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Robert Beverley on servants and slaves in Virginia, 1705
text: “Their Servants, they distinguish by the Names of Slaves for Life, and Servants for a time. Slaves are the Negroes, and their Posterity, following the condition of the Mother, according to the Maxim, partus sequitur ventrem [status follows the womb]. They are call’d Slaves, in respect of the time of their Servitude, because it is for Life. Servants, are those which serve only for a few years, according to the time of their Indenture, or the Custom of the Country. . . . The Male-Servants, and Slaves of both Sexes, are employed together in Tilling and Manuring the Ground, in Sowing and Planting Tobacco, Corn, &c.”
passages.attribution: Robert Beverley, a wealthy Virginia planter and enslaver, The History and Present State of Virginia, 1705. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 3.3.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/3-3-english-settlements-in-america); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of European empires in North America
text: “Europe's empires in North America took strikingly different shapes. New France stretched along rivers and lakes but held few settlers; its wealth came from furs that Native hunters supplied, so the French depended on alliances, gift-giving, and intermarriage. The Spanish built missions and presidios, seeking converts and labor, and faced fierce resistance, most dramatically in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680. The English, by contrast, arrived in large numbers, often as families, and wanted land to farm. That demand for land made conflict with American Indians far more likely.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the Great Awakening
text: “The revivals that swept the colonies in the 1730s and 1740s were more than a religious event. Traveling preachers drew enormous crowds from many colonies, speaking directly to ordinary people and urging them to judge the spiritual condition of their own ministers. Congregations split, new churches formed, and colonists learned that they could challenge established authority in the name of conscience. A generation later, some of the same habits of questioning would be turned against the British government.”
